Purpose: To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance, and to compare its performance to existing manual review practices.

Introduction: Accurate structuring and quality assurance of radiology reports are critical for patient care, yet manual review is time-consuming and prone to human error. Automated solutions, particularly those leveraging AI, have the potential to improve efficiency and consistency. However, most existing systems are cloud-based or single-agent, raising concerns about data privacy and limited error detection. Here, we present a novel, locally deployed multi-agent AI pipeline designed to structure radiology reports and flag clinically relevant errors, aiming to enhance report quality while preserving patient confidentiality.

Summary: We developed a multi-agent AI pipeline for structuring and quality assurance of radiology reports, evaluated its performance on 638 CT reports, and compared it to manual review by radiologists. The system achieved high accuracy in section assignment and error detection, with substantial time savings over manual review. Limitations include a small sample size for expert evaluation and potential generalizability issues. Our findings suggest that locally deployed multi-agent AI can improve report structuring and error detection, but further validation is needed.

Methods

Study Design and Dataset: This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists in 2023 and 2024. Reports were selected to represent a range of anatomical regions and clinical scenarios.

Multi-Agent AI Pipeline and Workflow: The pipeline consisted of three sequential agents (see Table 2 for a summary of the workflow):
1. Structuring Agent: Segmented reports into standardized anatomical sections at the sentence level using regular expression rules and a local large language model (LLM).
2. Consistency-Checking Agent: Detected mismatches between the Findings and Impression sections and within sections.
3. QA Agent: Identified gender-anatomy conflicts and undocumented communication of critical findings.

The workflow proceeded as follows: The structuring agent first assigned each sentence to an anatomical section, producing a structured report. This output was passed to the consistency-checking agent, which analyzed section content for mismatches. The QA agent then reviewed flagged outputs for gender-anatomy conflicts and undocumented critical findings. Each agent’s output served as the direct input for the next, and all processing was performed locally to ensure data privacy (see Table 2).

Table 2. Multi-Agent Workflow Summary

| Step | Agent                | Input                        | Output                                 | Next Step                |
|------|----------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| 1    | Structuring Agent    | Unstructured report          | Sentences assigned to anatomical sections | Consistency-Checking Agent |
| 2    | Consistency-Checking | Structured report            | Flagged section mismatches             | QA Agent                 |
| 3    | QA Agent             | Flagged outputs              | Gender-anatomy and communication errors| End                      |

Technical Details: The structuring agent used regular expressions to identify section headers (e.g., "Lungs:", "Liver:", "Kidneys:") and assign sentences accordingly. Sentences not matching predefined headers were processed by a local LLM based on the Llama-2-7B architecture, fine-tuned on 5,000 de-identified radiology reports from the same institution. The fallback logic was as follows: if a sentence did not match any regular expression header, it was passed to the LLM for section assignment. The LLM received as input a prompt of the form: "Assign the following sentence to the most appropriate anatomical section: [sentence]. Possible sections: [list]." The output was the predicted section label. Fine-tuning used an 80/20 training/validation split, a batch size of 16, learning rate of 2e-5, and 3 epochs on an NVIDIA A100 GPU running PyTorch 2.0 and CUDA 11.8. Hyperparameters were selected based on preliminary grid search for optimal validation accuracy, balancing overfitting and computational efficiency. Technical hyperparameters were selected to optimize validation accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency.

Manual Review Baseline: Manual review was conducted by two board-certified radiologists with at least five years of experience in abdominal and thoracic imaging. Reviewers were blinded to system outputs and received standardized training on the operational definitions and error criteria. Each radiologist independently reviewed the structuring and error flagging for each report. Disagreements were resolved by consensus discussion. The time required for manual review averaged 8 minutes per report. Inter-rater reliability was measured using Cohen’s kappa for both structuring and error flagging. For direct comparison, the AI system processed each report in under 10 seconds, representing a substantial time savings.

Error Flagging Criteria: Error types were selected based on their clinical relevance and frequency in prior quality assurance audits at our institution. The three error types were:
- "Section mismatch": A clinically relevant finding—defined as any abnormality or diagnosis with potential to alter patient management (e.g., pulmonary nodule, liver lesion, bowel obstruction, pneumothorax, active hemorrhage)—present in the Findings section but absent or contradictory in the Impression section, or vice versa. For example, a pulmonary nodule described in Findings but not mentioned in Impression, or an Impression stating "no acute findings" despite abnormal Findings, constituted a mismatch. Clinically significant errors were those likely to affect patient management, such as omission of a critical diagnosis from the Impression.
- "Gender-anatomy conflict": A report referenced anatomy inconsistent with the patient’s recorded gender (e.g., mention of "prostate" in a female patient, or "uterus" in a male patient).
- "Undocumented critical findings": A critical finding (e.g., pneumothorax, active hemorrhage, bowel perforation) was described in Findings but lacked documentation of communication in the Impression or a dedicated communication section. A critical finding was defined as one requiring urgent communication per institutional policy.

Examples of each error type are provided below for reproducibility:
- Section mismatch: Findings: "There is a 1.5 cm pulmonary nodule in the right upper lobe." Impression: "No acute findings."
- Gender-anatomy conflict: Report for a female patient states, "The prostate is unremarkable."
- Undocumented critical finding: Findings: "Large pneumothorax noted." Impression: "Right lung volume loss." No mention of communication.

Both radiologists reviewed and confirmed these operational definitions and example cases by consensus.

Sampling Strategy: For radiologist evaluation, 45 reports were selected using stratified random sampling to ensure representation of all flagged error types (section mismatches, gender-anatomy conflicts, undocumented critical findings) and anatomical regions (chest, abdomen, pelvis). The sample size of 45 was determined based on feasibility for expert review, aiming to include at least 10 examples of each error type and to balance reviewer workload. This sample size was a pragmatic choice to allow detailed consensus review, but it limits statistical power and generalizability, as reflected in wide confidence intervals. Larger samples would be needed for more robust estimates, and results should be interpreted with caution due to this limitation.

Evaluation Metrics: Evaluation metrics were defined as follows:
- "Correctly restructured": all sentences accurately assigned to the appropriate anatomical section, with no sentences omitted, fabricated, or assigned to an incorrect section, as determined by consensus radiologist review. For example, a sentence describing a liver lesion must appear in the "Liver" section and not in another section.
- "Incorrectly restructured": at least one sentence misassigned to the wrong section or clinical content altered (e.g., a bowel finding placed in the "Kidneys" section).
- QA performance ratings were defined quantitatively: "excellent" (0 errors, all flagged issues correctly identified, and no unflagged errors), "good" (1 minor error, such as a single missed or incorrectly flagged issue not affecting clinical interpretation), and "fair" (≥1 error with potential to affect clinical interpretation, such as missed critical findings or major section misassignments). A "minor error" was defined as a discrepancy that would not alter patient management or clinical interpretation, such as a typographical error or a missed non-critical finding. For reproducibility, a "minor error" was operationalized as a single missed or incorrectly flagged issue that would not change patient management, while a "major error" was any error likely to affect clinical interpretation or management.
- Inter-rater agreement was measured using Cohen’s kappa.
- System-level accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score were calculated against the radiologist consensus for each error type. Confidence intervals for these metrics were calculated using the Wilson score method.

A summary of key evaluation metrics is provided in Table 1.

Table 1. Summary of System Performance Metrics (with 95% Confidence Intervals)

| Error Type                    | Accuracy (95% CI) | Precision (95% CI) | Recall (95% CI) | F1-score (95% CI) |
|-------------------------------|------------------|--------------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Section mismatches            | 89% (76–96%)     | 81% (64–92%)       | 77% (60–89%)    | 79% (62–90%)      |
| Gender-anatomy conflicts      | 99% (91–100%)    | 100% (54–100%)     | 83% (36–99%)    | 91% (42–99%)      |
| Undocumented critical findings| 98% (89–100%)    | 80% (28–99%)       | 75% (22–99%)    | 77% (24–99%)      |
